london_system.name: London System
london_system.summary: A solid, easy-to-learn opening. You play the same setup almost every game. Bishop out before e3 — that's the golden rule.
golden_rules: Bishop to f4 first, before e3. Always.
Don't trade your dark bishop unless you get something big.
Your dream setup: d4, e3, Bf4, Nf3, Bd3, O-O.
After setup is done, push for e4.

traps.name: Englund Gambit Trap
traps.description: They play 1...e5 trying to trick you. Take the pawn and win.
traps.trap_idea: They try to take your b2 pawn with their queen. Let them — then trap the queen.
traps.how_to_avoid: Just play normal development. Their queen gets stuck.

traps.name: Bg4 Pin Trick
traps.description: They pin your knight spot with Bg4. You have a strong response.
traps.trap_idea: Push h3 then g4 to kick their bishop, then jump Ne5.
traps.how_to_avoid: Don't panic when they play Bg4. h3 then g4 is strong.

traps.name: Queen Trap after c5
traps.description: They take b2 with their queen. Nb5 and Rb1 traps it.
traps.trap_idea: Let them take b2. Their queen has no escape.
traps.how_to_avoid: Make sure you have Nb5 before allowing Qxb2.

d4.hint: What's the strongest first move to take the center?
d4.right_feedback: Good — d4 takes the center. Now think about your bishop.

d5.name: Main Line
d5.idea_opponent: They take their share of the center. Fair game.
d5.hint: Which piece should come out BEFORE you play e3?
d5.right_feedback: Exactly — Bf4 before e3. Golden rule of the London.
d5.wrong_feedback: In the London, the bishop MUST come to f4 before e3.

Nf6.hint: Same question as always — which piece first?
Nf6.right_feedback: Bf4 — doesn't matter what they play, bishop first.

Qb6.hint: Their queen eyes b2. How do you develop AND set a trap?
Qb6.right_feedback: Nc3 — if they take b2, Nb5+Rb1 traps their queen.

e5.name: Englund Gambit
e5.idea_opponent: A trick! They sacrifice a pawn hoping you blunder.
e5.hint: They offered a pawn. Should you take it?
e5.right_feedback: Take it. The Englund Gambit is bad for Black if you play correctly.
e5.wrong_feedback: Take the pawn! dxe5 is strong.

Bf5.name: Mirror London
Bf5.hint: They mirrored your London. Change your plan?
Bf5.right_feedback: e3 — stick to the plan. You have more space.

when_ahead.plan: Push e4 to open the center. Trade off defensive pieces.
ideas: Knight on e5 is a monster

when_equal.plan: Aim for e4. If blocked, play on the queenside with a4-a5.

when_behind.plan: Keep it closed. d4+e3 is hard to break. Wait for their mistake.

endgame_tips: d4+e3 structure is solid in endgames.
Activate your king early.
Push passed pawns.

italian_game.name: Italian Game
italian_game.summary: A classic opening. Develop quickly, point your bishop at f7, and attack the king. Simple and dangerous.
golden_rules: Bishop to c4 — aim at f7, the weakest square.
c3 prepares d4 — the ideal center.
Castle before attacking.
Don't take pawns if it loses time.

traps.name: Fried Liver Attack
traps.description: Knight goes to g5 attacking f7. If they take, you sacrifice the knight for a devastating attack.
traps.trap_idea: After Nxf7, their king is dragged out. The attack is crushing.
traps.how_to_avoid: Black should play d5 instead of allowing Ng5.

traps.name: Legal's Mate
traps.description: Sacrifice the queen to deliver checkmate with minor pieces.
traps.trap_idea: If they take your queen with Bxd1, you play Bxf7+ Ke7 Nd5#. Checkmate!
traps.how_to_avoid: Don't take the queen if you see Bxf7+ coming.

traps.name: Blackburne Shilling Gambit
traps.description: Black plays Nd4 hoping you take f7. Don't — just take the knight.
traps.trap_idea: Bxf7+ looks tempting but wastes your bishop. Nxd4 wins a piece.
traps.how_to_avoid: Don't be greedy. Nxd4 is simple and strong.

Nc6.name: Defending e5
Nc6.wrong_feedback: If you want the Italian Game, Bc4 is the move — aim at f7. Bb5 is the Ruy Lopez; d4 is the Scotch. Both fine, just different openings.

Bc5.name: Giuoco Piano
Bc5.hint: Prepare d4 with a pawn first.
Bc5.right_feedback: c3 — prepares d4. The big center is coming.
Bc5.wrong_feedback: In the Italian Game, the idea is: c3 prepares d4 — that's how you build the big center. Playing d4 immediately lets Black trade with exd4, hitting your knight and equalizing. d3 (the Giuoco Pianissimo / Italian Modern) is the quieter alternative — also OK if you prefer slow play, but c3 is the classical main line.

Nf6.name: Italian Main Line
Nf6.hint: Now you can play the central break.
Nf6.right_feedback: d4 — supported by c3. Now the big center is yours.
Nf6.wrong_feedback: In the Italian Game, d4 is the plan c3 was preparing. Anything else (b4 — Evans Gambit accepted is theoretically fine but a different opening; O-O — playable but lets Black play d6+ and consolidate) lets Black equalize.

exd4.name: Italian — d4 accepted
exd4.right_feedback: cxd4 — recapture with the c-pawn, building the big center.

Bb4+.name: Italian — Bb4+ check
Bb4+.idea_opponent: Black checks, hoping to disrupt your development.
Bb4+.right_feedback: Nc3 — block with the knight, accept the trade (or Bd2). Don't move the king.
Bb4+.wrong_feedback: In the Italian Game after cxd4 Bb4+, Nc3 is the natural block — develops a piece AND meets the check. Bd2 (MÃ¶ller Attack variations) is also fine if you want sharper play. Don't play Kf1 (loses castling) or Kd2 (insane).

Nge7.name: Hungarian-like setup with Nge7
Nge7.idea_opponent: Unusual — knight to e7 instead of f6.
Nge7.wrong_feedback: Against Black's passive Nge7, d4 immediately is fine — Black can't easily challenge the center with the knight on e7 (blocks the e-pawn). Calm Italian setup play wins here.

Be7.name: Hungarian Defense
Be7.idea_opponent: Black plays the solid, passive Hungarian.
Be7.hint: Black's setup is too quiet — strike the center immediately.
Be7.right_feedback: d4 — open the center. The Hungarian doesn't fight for it; punish that.
Be7.wrong_feedback: Against the Hungarian Defense (...Be7), d4 immediately is the best-known punishment — Black's quiet bishop on e7 lacks coordination with the rest of the army. d3 (slow Italian) is fine but lets Black equalize. d4 demands accuracy from Black.

Nf6.name: Two Knights Defense
Nf6.idea_opponent: Black plays more actively, eyes e4.
Nf6.right_feedback: Ng5 — attacks f7! Black must defend with d5 or face the Fried Liver.
Nf6.wrong_feedback: In the Two Knights Defense, Ng5 attacks f7 directly. d3 is the quiet Modern Italian (safer); d4 leads to the Max Lange or Scotch Gambit transpositions. Pick your style — but avoid Nc3 which lets Black equalize easily with d5.

d5.name: Two Knights — d5
d5.idea_opponent: Black blocks the diagonal, counter-attacks the bishop.

Nxd5.name: Fried Liver setup
Nxd5.idea_opponent: Black recaptures with the knight — runs into the Fried Liver.
Nxd5.right_feedback: Nxf7! — the Fried Liver Attack. Black's king is exposed.
Nxd5.wrong_feedback: After exd5 Nxd5, Nxf7 is THE move — the Fried Liver. Any other move lets Black escape. The point: Black's knight on d5 IS undefended; Nxf7 forces Kxf7 (the king can't run), then Qf3+ regains material and continues the attack.

Na5.name: Polerio Defense
Na5.idea_opponent: Black hits the bishop, sidestepping the Fried Liver.
Na5.right_feedback: Bb5+ — check, keeps the bishop active.
Na5.wrong_feedback: In the Polerio, Bb5+ is best-known — give check first, develop while gaining time. Retreating with Bb3 or Bf1 loses tempo. d3 (Bd3 next) is the quiet alternative — playable but less ambitious.

Nd4.name: Fritz Variation
Nd4.right_feedback: c3 — kick the knight, regain control of the center.
Nd4.wrong_feedback: In the Two Knights Fritz Variation, c3 kicks the d4 knight. Nxf7 here is INCORRECT (the knight on d4 isn't undefended like in the main line). c3 first, then the position becomes tactical.

italian_game_black.name: Italian Game (Black side)
italian_game_black.summary: How to defend against the Italian Game (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4) as Black. Two main systems: Two Knights Defense (3...Nf6 — sharp, attacking the e-pawn back) or Giuoco Piano (3...Bc5 — mirror the bishop, classical). Both are sound; choice depends on whether you want sharp or quiet play.
golden_rules: Against 3.Bc4, Nf6 (Two Knights) is the sharpest reply — counter-attack the e-pawn.
Bc5 (Giuoco Piano) mirrors White's bishop — solid, equal-ish.
Watch for the Fried Liver — d5 to block White's Ng5 is critical.
Don't play Na5 to chase the bishop unless you know the Polerio theory cold.

Bc4.name: Italian Game
Bc4.idea_opponent: White aims the bishop at f7.
Bc4.hint: Two Knights (sharp) or Bc5 (classical)? Nf6 is the most ambitious.
Bc4.right_feedback: Nf6 — the Two Knights Defense. Counter-attack e4. Sharper play ahead.
Bc4.wrong_feedback: Against the Italian (3.Bc4), Nf6 is the Two Knights Defense — counter-attacks White's e-pawn, leads to sharp tactical play (including the Fried Liver if White goes for it). Bc5 is the Giuoco Piano — mirror White's bishop, classical/equal. Both sound; Nf6 if you want sharper games.

Ng5.name: Italian — Fried Liver Attack
Ng5.idea_opponent: White attacks f7 with the knight!
Ng5.hint: Block the diagonal AND attack White's bishop. One move that does both?
Ng5.right_feedback: d5 — defend f7 by blocking the diagonal, AND counter-attack the bishop. The critical defense.
Ng5.wrong_feedback: Against 4.Ng5 (Fried Liver Attack), d5 is THE critical defense — blocks Bc4's diagonal at f7 AND attacks the bishop. Without d5, White plays 5.Nxf7 and your king is gutted. Other moves (Bc5, Nxe4) lose to the Fried Liver. d5 is mandatory.

exd5.name: Two Knights — d5 accepted
exd5.hint: DON'T recapture with the knight — that's the Fried Liver trap. Hit the bishop instead.
exd5.right_feedback: Na5 — the Polerio Defense. Attacks the bishop, sidesteps the Fried Liver.
exd5.wrong_feedback: After 5.exd5, Na5 (Polerio Defense) is the best-known move — hits Bc4 while gaining time, avoids the Fried Liver entirely. Nxd5 here is the Fried Liver trap — White plays Nxf7! winning material. Na5 is sound; Nxd5 is unsound unless you've memorized the Lolli/Traxler refutation lines.

d3.name: Italian — Modern (d3) / Giuoco Pianissimo
d3.idea_opponent: White plays the quiet Modern Italian — slow, long-term.
d3.right_feedback: Bc5 — mirror White's bishop, classical setup. Equal long-term game ahead.
d3.wrong_feedback: Against the Modern Italian (d3), Bc5 is the classical reply — mirror the bishop. d6 is also fine (Pirc-like). The Modern Italian is quiet; both sides have similar plans and the game is decided in the middlegame.

when_equal.plan: In the Italian as Black, the typical middlegame plan is queenside expansion (a6 + b5 + Bb7) while White attacks on the kingside. Trade pieces if needed.
ideas: Develop pieces actively, especially the c8 bishop via b7 or g4.
Castle kingside, then expand on the queenside with a6 + b5.
Watch for White's d4 break — meet it with exd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 cxd4 etc.

when_ahead.plan: Trade down. The Italian as Black usually reaches equal or slightly worse positions; if you're ahead, trade pieces and aim for the endgame.

when_behind.plan: Defend solidly — the Italian rarely produces forced losing lines from Black's side. Keep the position closed.

endgame_tips: Bishop endgames where you have the bishop pair are technically winning if you have any advantage.
Rook endgames after the Italian are often dry — know your Lucena and Philidor positions.

sicilian_defense.name: Sicilian Defense
sicilian_defense.summary: The sharpest response to e4. You fight for the center with c5 instead of e5. Leads to rich, complex positions.
golden_rules: c5 fights for d4 without committing your e-pawn.
You're playing for a queenside counter-attack.
Don't be scared of White's kingside attack — you attack queenside.
d6 + Nf6 is the solid setup.

traps.name: Siberian Trap
traps.description: Black plays Qa5 pinning the knight and threatening Bxc3+.
traps.trap_idea: White's knight on c3 is pinned. If they don't see it, you win material.
traps.how_to_avoid: White should play Bd2 or Nb3 to break the pin.

traps.name: Magnus Smith Trap
traps.description: White plays Bc4 and after Bg7, Nd5! forks everything.
traps.trap_idea: The knight on d5 attacks multiple pieces. Black's in trouble.
traps.how_to_avoid: Black should delay Bg7 and play a6 or e6 first.

e4.hint: What move fights for d4 from the flank, avoiding symmetry?
e4.right_feedback: c5 — the Sicilian. Most ambitious response to e4.
e4.wrong_feedback: In response to 1.e4, c5 is the Sicilian — most ambitious for Black, sets up unbalanced play. e5 invites the Open Game (Italian / Ruy Lopez / Scotch), e6 the French, c6 the Caro-Kann, d6 Pirc/Modern. All sound; c5 is the most fighting.

Nf3.name: Sicilian — Open setup begins
Nf3.idea_opponent: White's most popular move, preparing d4.
Nf3.hint: Flexible Najdorf-style setup — prepare Nf6 and later a6.
Nf3.right_feedback: d6 — supports e5 push, prepares Nf6.
Nf3.wrong_feedback: Against 2.Nf3, d6 is the most flexible — leads to Najdorf / Classical / Dragon depending on Black's later choices. Nc6 commits to the Classical / Sveshnikov lines. e6 leads to Taimanov / Kan / Paulsen. All sound; d6 is the most-played at top level.

d4.name: Open Sicilian
d4.right_feedback: cxd4 — trade pawns, open the c-file for queenside play.

Nc3.name: Open Sicilian — Nc3
Nc3.hint: Najdorf or Classical? a6 commits you to one of the most-studied openings in chess.
Nc3.right_feedback: a6 — the Najdorf. Prepare b5 + Bb7, fight on the queenside.
Nc3.wrong_feedback: In the Najdorf Sicilian, a6 prepares b5 + Bb7 — fighting on the queenside. Nc6 here would be the Classical Sicilian (different plan: knight to c6, dark-square strategy). g6 leads to the Dragon (sharp, double-edged). All sound; if you want the Najdorf, a6 is the move.

Be3.name: Najdorf — English Attack
Be3.idea_opponent: White plays the sharp English Attack — Be3, f3, g4, h4, attacking the kingside.
Be3.hint: Strike back in the center before White's pawn storm arrives.
Be3.right_feedback: e5 — closes the center, kicks the d4 knight, fights for d5 safe square.
Be3.wrong_feedback: In the Najdorf English Attack, e5 is the best-known central break — closes the center BEFORE White's kingside storm gets going. Nf6 already played; e6 (Scheveningen-style) is playable but invites a faster White attack. e5 is sharp but theoretically sound.

Bg5.name: Najdorf — Bg5
Bg5.idea_opponent: White plays the aggressive Bg5 main line.
Bg5.right_feedback: e6 — solidify the kingside, prepare Be7.
Bg5.wrong_feedback: Against the Bg5 Najdorf, e6 is the most-played response — solid, prepares ...Be7. ...Nbd7 is also OK but less precise. e5 (which works against English Attack) is INFERIOR here because Bg5 pins the f6 knight and the e5 push isn't easily prepared.

c3.name: Alapin (2.c3)
c3.idea_opponent: White props the centre with c3, planning d4 — dodging the Open Sicilian.
c3.hint: Strike the centre at once, before White gets in d4.
c3.right_feedback: d5 — hit back immediately. With the pawn on c3, White can't develop the knight to c3, so your queen won't get chased after the trade.
c3.wrong_feedback: Against the Alapin, d5 is the most reliable — strike the centre while White's c3 pawn blocks the natural Nc3 development. Nf6 (inviting 3.e5) is the other main try, but d5 is the simplest equaliser.

exd5.name: Alapin — Main
exd5.right_feedback: Qxd5 — and here it's safe: White has no Nc3 (the pawn's on c3), so your queen sits comfortably. Develop next.

d4.name: Smith-Morra Gambit
d4.idea_opponent: White offers a pawn (2.d4 cxd4 3.c3) for fast development and open lines.
d4.hint: Take the pawn — but you don't have to keep taking.
d4.right_feedback: cxd4 — take it. If White then plays c3 (the Morra), you can decline the second pawn and just develop.

c3.name: Smith-Morra — declined
c3.idea_opponent: White offers a second pawn for a big lead in development.
c3.hint: Develop and hit e4 instead of getting greedy.

bishops_opening.name: Bishops Opening
bishops_opening.summary: An old, healthy opening: the bishop goes to c4 before the knight comes to f3, keeping your f-pawn free and eyeing f7 from move two.
golden_rules: Bishop to c4 BEFORE knight to f3 — that's the whole point. Your f-pawn stays free to push later.
After ...Nf6, play d3 to protect e4. Quiet, solid, no tricks needed.
Don't rush Qh5 — against good defence it just loses time.
If Black plays ...Bc5, you can steer back into Italian waters with Nf3.

e5.name: Open Game
e5.idea_opponent: Black stakes the same claim in the center.
e5.right_feedback: Bc4 — bishop out first, aiming at f7. That's the Bishop's Opening.

Nf6.name: Berlin Defense
Nf6.idea_opponent: Black develops and attacks your e4 pawn straight away.
Nf6.hint: Your e4 pawn is attacked. Protect it with a pawn, keep developing.
Nf6.right_feedback: d3 — protects e4 with a pawn. Now knights and castling come next, and your f-pawn is still free to push f4 later.
Nf6.wrong_feedback: d3 is the move — it protects e4. Nf3 lets Black play Nxe4: after you win the pawn back the position is level and your c4 bishop has lost its bite.

Bc5.name: Classical setup
Bc5.right_feedback: Nf3 — develop toward the center; you're a tempo up on many Italian lines because d3 is already in.

d6.name: Solid center
d6.hint: Both bishops are out and the center is stable — what does your king want?
d6.right_feedback: Castles — king safe, rook ready. A calm, healthy position where you understand every piece's job.
d6.wrong_feedback: Castling is the priority here — the center is stable and every developing move works better with the king safe.

c6.name: Preparing d5
c6.right_feedback: Nf3 — keep developing. If Black pushes d5, exd5 cxd5 and the bishop drops back to b3 still watching that diagonal.
c6.wrong_feedback: Just develop with Nf3. Black wants ...d5; you meet it with exd5 and Bb3 — no need to stop it.

Bc5.name: Classical Defense
Bc5.idea_opponent: Black mirrors your bishop, also eyeing your weakest point f2.
Bc5.hint: Develop the kingside knight — you're back in familiar Italian territory.
Bc5.right_feedback: Nf3 — this steers into the Italian Game, which you already know: c3 and d4 is the plan.
Bc5.wrong_feedback: Nf3 is simplest — it turns the game into an Italian, where c3 and d4 give you the center.

Nc6.name: Knight development
Nc6.right_feedback: Nf3 — transposes to the Italian Game. Same ideas: c3, d4, castle short.
Nc6.wrong_feedback: Nf3 keeps it simple and turns this into an Italian Game you already know.

vienna_game.name: Vienna Game
vienna_game.summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3. Develop the queen's knight first, then choose: Vienna Gambit (3.f4) for sharp attacking play, Bc4 (Italian-style) for solid long-term play, or g3 (fianchetto) for hypermodern setups. Often transposes to Italian or King's Gambit territory.
golden_rules: Nc3 first, then commit: f4 (Vienna Gambit, sharp) or Bc4 (Italian-style, quiet).
The Vienna Gambit (3.f4) is sharp — only play it if you've studied the lines.
Bc4 + d3 + Nf3 + O-O is the calm path, transposes to Italian.
Don't play Bg5 too early — Black can chase the bishop with h6.

e5.name: Open Game
e5.hint: Develop the queen's knight first — the Vienna Game.
e5.right_feedback: Nc3 — Vienna Game. Develops the queen's knight before the king's knight.
e5.wrong_feedback: In the Vienna Game, Nc3 is the defining move — queen's knight first. Nf3 transposes to Italian/Ruy/Scotch (all fine, just different openings). Bc4 leads to Bishop's Opening. For the Vienna, Nc3 first.

Nf6.name: Vienna — Main
Nf6.hint: Italian-style: aim the bishop at f7. Or play f4 (Vienna Gambit) for sharp attack.
Nf6.right_feedback: Bc4 — quiet Vienna. Now plan d3 + Nf3 + O-O. (f4 is the Vienna Gambit — sharper alternative.)
Nf6.wrong_feedback: Against 2...Nf6, you have a real choice: Bc4 (quiet, Italian-style) or f4 (Vienna Gambit — sharp, theoretically OK but requires study). g3 (Fianchetto) is also valid. Pick based on style. For 1200-1500 players, Bc4 is the safer choice.

when_equal.plan: Develop calmly: d3 + Nf3 + O-O + Nbd2 + Re1. Vienna positions are slow long-term games unless you commit to the Gambit.
ideas: Don't push f4 unless you have a clear attacking plan.
Trade the bishop on c4 for Black's knight only if you get something concrete.
Build up slowly with f3 + g3 + h3 + Kg2 as the king cluster.

when_ahead.plan: Push f4-f5 to expand on the kingside. Vienna structures naturally lead to kingside attacks.
ideas: Push f4 then f5 to open lines.
Sacrifice pieces for the king attack if calculation works.

when_behind.plan: Trade pieces, simplify. The Vienna is rarely lost from solid positions.

endgame_tips: Vienna endings often resemble Italian — same pawn structures, same plans.
Bishop pair is the key asset if you keep both.
vienna_game.white_plan: Prepare f4 (Vienna Gambit) or Bc4 for attacking play, delay Nf3 for flexibility
vienna_game.black_plan: Develop naturally with Nf6, be ready for f4 gambit, maintain central presence

vienna_gambit.name: Vienna Gambit
vienna_gambit.white_plan: Gambit f4 for open lines, develop quickly, attack the kingside
vienna_gambit.black_plan: Accept with d5! Counter in the center, develop actively, castle quickly

after_f4.key_decision: The gambit! Black must respond precisely

d5.idea: Counter in the center - the strongest response!
d5.why_good: Opens the position while Black is better developed

exf4.why_bad: Accepting passively gives White a strong center
exf4.consequence: After e5, White has a powerful center and open f-file
exf4.learning: Against gambits, counter in the CENTER (d5) rather than just taking pawns

vienna_bc4.name: Vienna Game - Bc4 System
vienna_bc4.white_plan: Develop Bc4 and f4, combine Italian-style play with Vienna flexibility
vienna_bc4.black_plan: Develop Nc6, Bc5, counter with d6 and Bg4 pin, castle early

after_Bc4.key_decision: White combines Bc4 with Nc3 - more flexible than the Italian

Nc6.why_good: Prepares Bc5 and keeps options open

Nxe4.why_good: Tactical shot - after Nxe4, Qh5! forks

after_Nc3.key_decision: Black chooses between Nf6 (solid) or Nc6 (classical)

Nf6.why_good: The most active response, challenging White's center

Nc6.why_good: Solid - develops a piece and supports e5

common_learnings: The Vienna delays Nf3 to keep f4 options open
Against f4, counter with d5 in the center - don't just take the pawn
Bc4 systems combine Italian themes with Vienna flexibility
White aims for quick piece activity; Black should counter-punch in the center

englund_gambit_response.name: Englund Gambit Response
englund_gambit_response.summary: After 1.d4 e5 (Englund Gambit by Black), the best-known response is 2.dxe5 — accept the pawn. Black doesn't get much back for it; if they try the Englund Gambit Mate Trap (2...Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Bf4?? Qb4+ winning the b2 pawn or worse), white must NOT play 4.Bf4. Develop normally with 3.Nf3 and 4.Nc3 or 4.Bf4-with-care.
golden_rules: Accept the gambit: 2.dxe5 — take the pawn.
Watch for the Englund Mate Trap: after 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7, do NOT play 4.Bf4 (loses to Qb4+).
Develop calmly with Nf3 + Nc3 + e3 — don't try to keep all the extra material.
Black usually doesn't get much back for the pawn — convert the endgame patiently.

e5.name: Englund Gambit
e5.idea_opponent: Black sacrifices the e-pawn for dubious the attack.
e5.hint: Take the pawn. Black's gambit is theoretically losing.
e5.right_feedback: dxe5 — accept the gambit. Black doesn't get much back for it.
e5.wrong_feedback: Against the Englund Gambit (1...e5), dxe5 is the best-known response — take the pawn. The Englund is theoretically unsound; you should win a pawn cleanly. Refusing with c4 or Nf3 is OK but accepting is sharper.

Qe7.name: Englund — Mate Trap attempt
Qe7.idea_opponent: Black sets up the Englund Mate Trap (Qb4+ next).
Qe7.hint: Develop the queen's knight — and AVOID Bf4 which loses to Qb4+.
Qe7.right_feedback: Nc3 — develop safely. NOT Bf4 (which would lose to Qb4+ winning b2 pawn or queen).
Qe7.wrong_feedback: In the Englund Mate Trap, Nc3 is correct. Bf4?? is the famous trap — Black plays Qb4+ and you lose the b2 pawn (or worse, the queen if you block with Qd2 Qxb2 winning). Nc3 develops safely AND defends b4 indirectly.

when_equal.plan: Convert the extra pawn. Trade pieces, simplify, win the endgame.

when_ahead.plan: You're up a pawn from the start. Push the queenside majority in the endgame.
ideas: Push a4-a5 or b4 to create a passed pawn.
Trade pieces to reach a winning endgame.

when_behind.plan: Shouldn't happen if you avoided the Englund Mate Trap. If it does, defend solidly.

endgame_tips: Up-a-pawn endings: trade pieces, push passed pawns.
The Englund Gambit's pawn advantage typically persists into the endgame.

kings_gambit.name: King's Gambit
kings_gambit.summary: 1.e4 e5 2.f4. You offer the f-pawn to tear open the centre and the f-file for a fast attack on Black's king. Sharp and fun — strongest when you know the first few moves. After 2...exf4, play 3.Nf3 (it stops the queen check on h4), aim the bishop at f7 with Bc4, castle, and attack.
golden_rules: After Black takes on f4, play Nf3 at once — it stops the queen check on h4.
Aim the light bishop at f7 (Bc4) and castle quickly; the open f-file is your attacking lane.
Don't chase the pawn back on f4 — finish developing and open lines instead.
If Black hits back with 2...d5, take with exd5 and keep developing — don't panic.

e5.name: Open Game
e5.idea_opponent: Black claims their share of the centre.
e5.hint: Offer the f-pawn — 2.f4, the King's Gambit.
e5.right_feedback: f4 — the King's Gambit. You give up a pawn to rip open the centre and aim at f7.
e5.wrong_feedback: For the King's Gambit the move is f4 — offering the pawn to blast the centre open. Nf3 is the calm Italian/Ruy path instead (also fine, just not the gambit).

exf4.name: King's Gambit Accepted
exf4.idea_opponent: Black takes the pawn on f4.
exf4.hint: Play Nf3 — it stops Black's queen from checking on h4.
exf4.right_feedback: Nf3 — the key move. It covers h4 (no more queen check) and develops toward the kingside.
exf4.wrong_feedback: Develop with Nf3 first. Skip it and Black plays Qh4+, dragging your king out before you're ready. Nf3 covers h4 and brings a piece out.

g5.name: Classical Defence
g5.idea_opponent: Black props up the extra pawn with g5.
g5.right_feedback: h4 — challenge the g5 pawn before Black builds a wall of pawns.

d5.name: Modern Defence
d5.idea_opponent: Black hits the centre back instead of holding the pawn.
d5.right_feedback: exd5 — open the centre while you're ahead in development.

Nf6.name: Schallopp Defence
Nf6.idea_opponent: Black develops and eyes the e4 pawn.
Nf6.right_feedback: e5 — push the pawn, take space and kick the knight.

Bc5.name: Classical Declined
Bc5.idea_opponent: Black declines and points the bishop at g1, making your castling awkward.
Bc5.hint: Just develop with Nf3 — don't take on e5.
Bc5.right_feedback: Nf3 — develop. Taking fxe5 here opens lines for Black's queen with Qh4+ ideas.
Bc5.wrong_feedback: Develop with Nf3. Taking fxe5 lets Black play Qh4+ and chase your king. Keep it solid and bring pieces out.

d5.name: Falkbeer Counter-Gambit
d5.idea_opponent: Black counter-attacks the centre instead of taking on f4.
d5.hint: Take the pawn — exd5 — then develop calmly.
d5.right_feedback: exd5 — take it, then finish your development. Don't cling to the pawn; get your pieces out.
d5.wrong_feedback: Take with exd5. Against the Falkbeer, taking the pawn and developing is simplest — fxe5 instead lets Black's pieces flood out with the lead.

when_equal.plan: Finish developing toward the king: Nf3 + Bc4 + O-O, then aim down the open f-file at f7. The half-open f-file is the whole point of the gambit.
ideas: Double rooks on the f-file once the king is castled.
Use the d4 pawn break to open the centre when your king is safer than Black's.
Win the f4 pawn back later if it's free, but never at the cost of development.

when_ahead.plan: Open lines and attack — push d4 and bring everything at the king. A development lead in the King's Gambit is meant to be cashed in fast.
ideas: Sacrifice the gambit pawn (or another) to open the f-file and the centre.
Bring the rook to f1 and the knight to g5/e5 toward f7.

when_behind.plan: If the attack fizzles and you're just down the pawn, trade pieces and head for an endgame where the extra pawn matters least.
ideas: Trade queens to kill Black's attacking chances.
Keep your pawns connected; avoid more weaknesses around the king.

endgame_tips: If you never won the f4 pawn back, you may be a pawn down — trade into rook endings where one pawn is hardest to convert.
Open f-file rooks stay strong into the endgame; keep at least one rook active.

four_knights_game.name: Four Knights Game
four_knights_game.summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6. Both sides bring both knights out — a calm, classical, very safe way to play 1.e4. Aim the bishop at b5 (Spanish-style), castle, and play a sound game with a tiny edge from the extra move.
golden_rules: Knights before bishops: Nf3 and Nc3 first, then decide where the bishop goes.
Bb5 copies the Ruy Lopez — it leans on the c6 knight that guards e5.
Castle early and keep the position solid; the Four Knights rarely blows up.
If Black pins your c3 knight with Bb4, you can mirror with Bb5 — symmetry is fine.

e5.name: Open Game
e5.hint: Develop the king's knight and hit the e5 pawn.
e5.right_feedback: Nf3 — develop and attack e5, the natural start.
e5.wrong_feedback: Start with Nf3 — develop a piece and put a question to the e5 pawn. That's the backbone of every 1.e4 e5 opening.

Nc6.name: Two Knights territory
Nc6.hint: Bring the queen's knight out too — heading for the Four Knights.
Nc6.right_feedback: Nc3 — both knights out. This is the Four Knights, calm and solid.
Nc6.wrong_feedback: Nc3 develops your second knight and defends e4 — the Four Knights. (Bc4 is the Italian, also fine; Bb5 is the Ruy. For the Four Knights, Nc3.)

Nf6.name: Four Knights — Main
Nf6.idea_opponent: Black develops symmetrically and eyes e4.
Nf6.right_feedback: Bb5 — Spanish-style. You lean on the c6 knight that holds e5. Castle next.

when_equal.plan: Finish developing and castle: Bb5 + O-O + d3 + Bg5. The Four Knights is a slow build — small, safe edges, no early fireworks.
ideas: Trade the b5 bishop for the c6 knight only when it wins something or wrecks Black's pawns.
Use the d4 or Nd5 break in the centre when your pieces are ready.
Keep the position symmetrical if you're happy with a small, safe edge.

when_ahead.plan: Open the centre with d4 once you're developed and use the extra tempo to push.
ideas: Jump a knight to d5 to pressure Black's position.

when_behind.plan: Symmetry is your friend — trade pieces and steer toward an equal endgame.

endgame_tips: Four Knights endings are usually balanced — the bishop pair is the asset to fight for.
Doubled c-pawns (if you take on c6) can be a long-term target either way; know which side they help.

pirc_defense.name: Pirc Defense (Classical System)
pirc_defense.summary: Black plays d6 and g6 and lets you build a big pawn centre, planning to chip at it later. The simplest reply is the Classical: take the centre with e4 + d4, develop Nc3 + Nf3 + Be2, castle, and hold your space. Don't overpush — let the extra space do the work.
golden_rules: Take the whole centre — e4 and d4 — when Black plays the modest d6/g6 setup.
Classical and calm: Nc3 + Nf3 + Be2 + O-O. You don't need a sharp attack to keep your edge.
Defend e4 with Nc3 before Black's pressure builds.
Hold your centre; don't lash out with early pawn pushes that create weaknesses.

d6.name: Pirc / Modern setup
d6.idea_opponent: Black invites you to build a big centre, planning to hit it later with pieces and ...e5/...c5.
d6.hint: Take the full centre while you can.
d6.right_feedback: d4 — take the big centre. The Pirc invites this; now develop and hold it.
d6.wrong_feedback: Take the centre with d4. Black's d6/g6 plan deliberately gives you space — accept it, then develop solidly.

Nf6.name: Pirc — attacking e4
Nf6.idea_opponent: Black develops and pokes your e4 pawn.
Nf6.hint: Defend e4 and develop the queen's knight.
Nf6.right_feedback: Nc3 — defends e4 and develops. Solid and natural.

g6.name: Pirc — Main
g6.idea_opponent: Black tucks the bishop to the side to g7, aiming at your centre.
g6.hint: Calm development — knight to f3, then bishop and castle (the Classical).
g6.right_feedback: Nf3 — the Classical system. Be2 and O-O next; keep your big centre.

Bg7.name: Pirc — Classical
Bg7.idea_opponent: Black's bishop eyes your centre down the long diagonal.
Bg7.right_feedback: Be2 — modest and solid. Castle next and sit on your space.

when_equal.plan: You have more space — develop everything, castle, and slowly improve. Re1, Bf4/Be3, Qd2. Don't rush; space wins slow games.
ideas: Meet Black's ...e5 or ...c5 break by keeping the centre solid, not panicking.
Trade Black's good g7 bishop with Be3 + Qd2 + Bh6 if you can.
Use your space to manoeuvre; avoid trades that relieve Black's tight position.

when_ahead.plan: Expand with the extra space — push in the centre or on the kingside once you're fully developed.
ideas: Consider a kingside pawn storm if Black has castled there.
Open the centre when your pieces are better placed.

when_behind.plan: Hold the centre and trade pieces; your space gives you a cushion even when worse.
ideas: Don't create pawn weaknesses around your king.

endgame_tips: Your extra central space often means a freer endgame — keep rooks active on open files.
Watch Black's ...c5/...e5 breaks; meeting them cleanly keeps your structure healthy into the ending.

alekhine_defense.name: Alekhine Defense
alekhine_defense.summary: 1.e4 Nf6. You poke the e4 pawn straight away and invite White to push pawns forward and chase your knight. The plan: let White build a big centre, hop the knight to safety, then strike back at the overextended pawns with d6 and c5. Provocative but fun.
golden_rules: 1...Nf6 dares White to chase you — when the pawn comes to e5, hop to d5, not back home.
After Nd5, strike at White's big centre with d6 — don't let those pawns settle.
Trade off White's e5 spearhead pawn (dxe5) to free your pieces.
Develop the light-square bishop actively (often Bg4 or Bf5) before locking it in.

e4.hint: Which knight move attacks the e4 pawn at once and dares White to chase it?
e4.right_feedback: Nf6 — the Alekhine. You poke e4 and invite White to overextend.

e5.name: Alekhine — the Chase
e5.idea_opponent: White kicks the knight and takes space.
e5.hint: Where does the knight go to stay safe AND active — not back to where it came from?
e5.right_feedback: Nd5 — hop forward, out of the pawn's reach. Retreating to g8 would waste the whole idea.
e5.wrong_feedback: Jump to d5 — forward, not back. Ng8 undoes your first move; Nd5 keeps the knight active and central while White's pawns hang in the air.

d4.name: Alekhine — Modern
d4.idea_opponent: White builds a broad pawn centre and dares you to break it.
d4.hint: Strike at the centre before it rolls over you.
d4.right_feedback: d6 — hit White's centre right away, before those pawns get comfortable.

Nf3.name: Alekhine — Modern Main
Nf3.idea_opponent: White develops calmly, trying to keep the big centre.
Nf3.right_feedback: dxe5 — trade off White's spearhead pawn and free your game.

when_equal.plan: You traded space for targets — White's advanced pawns are weaknesses if you keep hitting them. Develop actively (Bg4/Bf5, e6, Be7, O-O) and pile on the centre with c5.
ideas: Pressure White's d4/e5 pawns with pieces and the ...c5 break.
Get your light-square bishop out BEFORE ...e6 locks it in.
Castle and complete development; don't take pawns while behind in pieces.

when_ahead.plan: If White's centre has cracked, open lines and target the weak pawns directly.
ideas: Open the position to exploit White's loose pawns.
Trade into endings where the weak pawns fall.

when_behind.plan: If White's space holds, stay solid and look for one clean break (...c5 or ...f6) to free yourself.
ideas: Trade pieces to reduce White's space advantage.
Avoid passive piece shuffles — find a pawn break.

endgame_tips: If White's e5/d4 pawns survive into the endgame, blockade them with a knight on d5 or e6.
Your queenside majority can become a passed pawn once the centre is traded away.

englund_accepted.name: Englund Gambit Accepted
englund_accepted.white_plan: Take the free pawn with dxe5, then develop normally — Nf3 to hold the e5 pawn, Nc3 to cover the b4 square. Keep the extra pawn and steer toward a better endgame.
englund_accepted.black_plan: Try to win back e5 with tricks (Qe7 hits the pawn) and hope White runs into the famous Qb4+ trap.

after_qe7.key_decision: Black's queen on e7 attacks the e5 pawn and sets the trap. White must develop while keeping the b4 square covered.

Nc3.idea: Develop the knight AND cover b4.
Nc3.why_good: Stops the Qb4+ trick, defends the e-pawn indirectly, and keeps White a clean pawn up.

Bf4.why_bad: The famous Englund trap — the natural-looking 4.Bf4?? walks straight into Qb4+.
Bf4.consequence: After 4...Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 Black wins the b-pawn and hits the rook on a1; in the main line (6.Bc3 Bb4 7.Qd2 Bxc3 8.Qxc3 Qc1#) it's even checkmate.
Bf4.learning: When the enemy queen sits on e7 and your b2 pawn is loose, check for Qb4+ before you develop the bishop. Cover b4 first with Nc3.

nimzowitsch_defense.name: Nimzowitsch Defense
nimzowitsch_defense.white_plan: Maintain the center with d4, develop naturally, punish the unusual move order
nimzowitsch_defense.black_plan: Hypermodern approach - let White build the center, then attack it with d5, f5, or e5

nimzo_main.name: Nimzowitsch Main Line
nimzo_main.white_plan: Push e5 for space, develop Nf3-Be2-O-O, maintain the center
nimzo_main.black_plan: Challenge e5 with f6, develop Bf5 (before e6!), castle and counterattack

after_e5.key_decision: White has a space advantage with e5

Bf5.why_good: Active bishop, prepares f6 to challenge e5

e6.consequence: Black is tight with no active piece play
e6.learning: Always develop bishops before playing e6 in closed positions

nimzo_nf3.name: Nimzowitsch vs Nf3
nimzo_nf3.white_plan: Develop while gaining time against the queen, build a solid center
nimzo_nf3.black_plan: Transpose to Scandinavian-like positions, develop actively

Nc3.why_good: Standard - forces the queen to move again

after_Nc6.key_decision: White should take the center with d4

d4.idea: Occupy the center - the most best-known
d4.why_good: Takes advantage of Black's unusual move order

common_learnings: The Nimzowitsch Defense is a surprise weapon - opponents won't know the theory
Nc6 on move 1 is unusual but not bad - it has hypermodern ideas
Black often transposes into other openings (Scandinavian, French) from this setup

four_knights.summary: All four knights come out before anything else happens. Calm, symmetrical, and full of small traps for the side that stops paying attention.
golden_rules: Develop knights before bishops — this opening is the principle in its purest form.
Against the symmetrical setup, Bb5 (the Spanish Four Knights) is your simplest plan: pressure e5, castle, play d3.
d4 in one go (the Scotch Four Knights) is also fine: trade in the center and develop fast.
Don't take the e5 pawn with the knight — the fork trick d4 does NOT win it back cleanly here.

Nf6.name: Four Knights Game
Nf6.hint: All four knights are out. Which bishop move puts real pressure on the center?
Nf6.right_feedback: Bb5 — the Spanish Four Knights. You press the knight that defends e5; castle next and play d3. (d4, the Scotch Four Knights, is just as good.)
Nf6.wrong_feedback: Bb5 or d4 are the moves that fight for something. Taking on e5 with the knight is the one real mistake here — after Nxe5 Nxe5 d4, Black keeps the extra piece with Bd6 protecting the knight.

O-O.name: Both castled

O-O.wrong_feedback: d3 first — protect the e4 pawn and free your dark bishop. The Bg5 pin comes one move later.

Bc5.name: Active bishop
Bc5.hint: Black's bishop left b4-d6 unguarded... now the old fork trick DOES work.
Bc5.right_feedback: Nxe5! Now it works: after Nxe5 d4 forks bishop and knight and you win the pawn back with a better position.
Bc5.wrong_feedback: Here Nxe5 is the strong move — with the bishop on c5, d4 next forks bishop and knight, and you regain the piece with a extra central pawn.
